name: Phenotype maxxing

card.summary: A looksmaxxing framework of refining one's look toward a desirable phenotype, or an eye-catching feature within one's own ethnic range, using styling, colouring and sometimes surgery.
card.note: Some plans discussed involve surgery or eye-colour procedures with their own medical risks.

quick.overview:
Phenotype maxxing (also written phenomaxxing) is a term used on looksmaxxing forums for shaping one's appearance toward a chosen phenotype, meaning a recognisable cluster of inherited traits such as skin tone, eye colour, bone structure and hair. Practitioners aim to look like a more admired or more striking version of their own ancestry, or like a different phenotype they find appealing.

The payoff, as members describe it, is a more distinctive and harmonious overall look: colouring that contrasts well, a standout feature, or a facial impression that reads as a particular ethnicity. The idea is discussed through forum guides and personal plans rather than formal research, although members borrow concepts such as optimal distinctiveness from psychology.
quick.how: Threads describe mostly cosmetic levers: skin and lip colouring, hair colour and highlights, eyebrow shaping, coloured contact lenses and blush. More involved plans mention jaw or chin surgery and cosmetic eye-colour procedures. Members typically start by comparing photos of the phenotype they want with their own features.
quick.risks: Cosmetic contacts, skin-lightening products, eye-colour procedures and facial surgery each carry their own medical risks and are discussed by clinicians separately. Some forum participants also push back on specific suggestions, and views on what counts as an attractive phenotype differ widely.

lead: Phenotype maxxing, also called phenomaxxing, is a looksmaxxing framework in which a person refines how they look so that their features, colouring and proportions read as a more desirable phenotype. Some members aim for the best version of their own ancestry; others describe plans to approximate a different look they find appealing.[1][2] The word borrows from biology: a phenotype is an organism's observable traits, which result from its genotype together with environmental factors.[3]

Forum posts describe the toolkit in practical terms: attention to skin and lip colour, hair colour and highlights, tidy eyebrows, blush and lighter or coloured contact lenses, and in more ambitious plans a cosmetic eye-colour laser procedure combined with chin surgery.[1] Circle and tinted lenses, which are sold widely in East Asia and elsewhere, are one of the most accessible levers.[8]

A looksmax.org theory post argues that attractiveness rises when a person has one or two features that are unusual for their phenotype, citing the social-psychology concept of optimal distinctiveness alongside findings that average faces are rated attractive.[2] The first concept was proposed by Marilynn Brewer in 1991 to describe how people balance belonging and distinctiveness in group membership, and the second goes back to Galton's composite photographs and the 1990 Langlois and Roggman study.[7][4] Applying either to individual facial features is the posters' own extension; the literature does not test deliberate phenotype modification.

chain: Pick a target phenotype or a standout feature
Adjust colouring, hair, brows, lenses or structure
A more distinctive, coherent overall look
angle.text: Members use phenotype maxxing to plan which features to emphasise or change, mostly through colouring and grooming, and in some plans through surgery. The aim is a look that reads as more striking or more in line with a chosen ideal.[1][2]

infobox: Colour analysis, eyebrow and hair styling, cosmetic contact lenses[8]

paras: A phenotype is the observable set of traits a person shows, such as skin tone, eye colour, hair texture, brow projection and bone depth. Biology defines it as the observable result of genotype plus environment; Wilhelm Johannsen drew the genotype-phenotype distinction in 1911, and because development involves gene-environment interactions, phenotypic variation in a population exceeds genetic variation.[3]

In looksmaxxing usage, phenotype maxxing means working toward a preferred configuration of these traits. Threads use the word in two overlapping ways. One is optimising within the range of one's own ethnic group, for instance by choosing colouring and features that sit at the favourable end of that range. The other is adopting traits associated with another group, a goal that members themselves debate.[1][2]

Averageness. The finding that composites of many faces are rated more attractive than most of the faces that went into them dates to Francis Galton's composite photographs in 1878, and Langlois and Roggman reported in 1990 that composites of 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 faces became progressively more attractive, with the 32-face composite rated highest. Later work found that averages of already attractive faces were rated higher than averages of a general sample, and that caricaturing a face (exaggerating its differences from the mean) also raised attractiveness, giving a younger-looking face with larger eyes and a narrower jaw. The effect was found with Hadza participants in Tanzania in 2007 as well as European and Japanese raters.[4]

Symmetry and other cues. Wikipedia's summaries describe symmetry, averageness and youthfulness as shaping attractiveness judgments, with symmetry and averageness contributing independently.[5] Skin colour and texture preferences are reported as variable: one 2010 study found a preference for lighter but not lightest skin in New Zealand and California, while clear, smooth skin and vivid colour are cited as important across studies. Studies of eye features have found medium upper-eyelid creases rated most attractive in Chinese-descent women and wider eyes relative to facial height associated with higher ratings.[6]

Optimal distinctiveness. Brewer's 1991 theory holds that people seek a balance between inclusion and distinctiveness in group membership, with excessive distinctiveness risking stigma. It was developed for social identity and has been applied to stereotypes, self-esteem and marketing.[7] Forum posts apply the phrase to faces, describing attractive people as combining familiar proportions with one rare feature.[2]

The distinctiveness argument holds that attractive people tend to carry a rare feature, such as an unusual orbital shape or striking contrast between eye depth and skin clarity, set within otherwise typical proportions. The post names well-known actors as examples and argues that one unphenotypical feature can raise attractiveness a great deal.[2]

Members also describe phenotype work as a choice among 'looks': one thread describes a plan to look more like a particular regional phenotype after being repeatedly mistaken for another, through eye-colour depigmentation and genioplasty.[1] Other members in these communities reply with disagreement on particular suggestions, and the aims are contested within the forums themselves.[1][2]

Described approaches range from grooming and cosmetic colour changes to elective procedures. Examples in forum plans include cosmetic lenses, blush and lip colour, hair colour, brow shaping, an eye-colour laser procedure and genioplasty.[1] Circle lenses make the iris look larger with a visible limbal ring and have been sold since about 2004, especially in South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and China; in the US decorative lenses are regulated as medical devices requiring clearance and a prescription, and a meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia found tinted lenses appear safe when prescribed and used correctly.[8]

Members typically begin by comparing photographs of a target look with their own features, then decide which levers are cosmetic and reversible (colouring, lenses, hair) and which are surgical or procedural.

Each lever carries its own medical risks and is covered by clinicians separately. Wikipedia notes that poorly fitted tinted soft lenses can temporarily reduce vision in bright and dim light and that US concern centres on lenses bought without an optometrist's fitting.[8] Elective facial surgery and eye-colour procedures carry the general risks of surgery and ophthalmic procedures, and plans that rely on them are discussed on forums by members of widely varying experience.[1]
No studies found. Related psychology literature on facial averageness, symmetry and distinctiveness exists, but no published trials have tested phenotype maxxing as a practice.[4][5]

timeline.event: Francis Galton publishes composite photographs and notes that composites look more attractive than their component faces.[4]
Wilhelm Johannsen distinguishes genotype from phenotype.[3]
Langlois and Roggman report that composites of more faces are rated more attractive in a study of 192 faces.[4]
Marilynn Brewer proposes optimal distinctiveness theory in social psychology.[7]
Perrett and colleagues find that caricaturing a face increases its attractiveness.[4]
Circle contact lenses begin to be sold, becoming popular in East Asia.[8]
Apicella and colleagues test the averageness effect with the Hadza people of Tanzania.[4]
Leonardelli, Pickett and Brewer publish a major review of optimal distinctiveness theory.[7]

lore.intro: The term appears in looksmax.org threads containing personal plans and theory posts.[1][2]

claims.claim: A rare feature for one's phenotype raises attractiveness
claims.believers: Posters cite optimal distinctiveness and give examples of well-known actors with one striking feature.[2]
claims.experts: Optimal distinctiveness theory was developed for group membership rather than faces.[7] Research on faces has found both an averageness preference and an increase in attractiveness from caricaturing an average face.[4] No study has tested deliberately adding unphenotypical features.

claims.claim: Average faces are the most attractive
claims.believers: The theory post cites studies that average faces are rated attractive and treats averageness and distinctiveness as complementary.[2]
claims.experts: Langlois and Roggman found composites more attractive in 1990; later work found averages of attractive faces rated higher than averages of general samples, and symmetry and averageness contribute independently.[4][5]

claims.claim: Colouring changes can make a person look more attractive
claims.believers: Posters describe lip and cheek colour, hair highlights and lighter lenses as raising the overall impression.[1]
claims.experts: Studies report variable preferences for skin tone across populations, with clear skin and vivid colour often cited as important.[6]

claims.claim: Lighter or coloured eyes improve the overall phenotype
claims.believers: Members plan to use contact lenses or an eye-colour laser procedure to change iris colour.[1]
claims.experts: Circle and tinted lenses are cleared as medical devices in the US with a prescription; a meta-analysis found tinted lenses appear safe when prescribed and used correctly.[8] No study has tested whether lighter eyes raise attractiveness.

claims.claim: Work is done within a range set by one's ancestry
claims.believers: The theory post says that within any ethnic group there is a range of bone depth, brow projection, eye aperture and pigmentation, and that one can sit at a rare combination point.[2]
claims.experts: Biology treats phenotype as the product of genotype and environment, so variation within a population is wider than genetic variation alone.[3]

claims.claim: A different group's look can be approximated with surgery and colouring
claims.believers: One plan combines eye-colour change and chin surgery to look more like another regional phenotype.[1]
claims.experts: No published study has evaluated this goal; surgical and ophthalmic procedures are assessed individually by clinicians.
